issues.title: Availability is presented, but actual booking confidence is weak
issues.detail: The primary conversion mechanism is labeled “CHECK AVAILABILITY,” yet the page states that dates and final terms are confirmed directly by Mfinity. This makes the interaction feel like a lead form rather than a reservation flow, despite the site’s rental positioning.
issues.evidence: The hero form asks for “FROM,” “TO” and “VEHICLE,” then uses “CHECK AVAILABILITY.” The supporting copy says, “Dates and final terms are confirmed directly by Mfinity.” The objective scan reports a bookingSignalCount of 0 and a critical journey that does not fail, but does not identify a booking signal.
issues.observed: Visitors are not told whether submitting the form creates a reservation request, starts a quote, or simply sends an enquiry. There is no visible confirmation of next steps, response time or reservation status.
issues.expected: Reference-quality rental UX should make the transaction model explicit: instant availability, quote request, or concierge reservation. The customer should know what happens after submission and how quickly Mfinity will respond.
issues.location: Desktop and mobile hero availability form and adjacent explanatory copy.
issues.recommendation: Rename and frame the action around the real process, for example “REQUEST RESERVATION” or “GET AVAILABILITY & PRICE,” then state the next step and response expectation directly below it. Add a clear confirmation state after submission.

issues.title: The page lacks visible trust proof for a high-value rental decision
issues.detail: Luxury vehicle rental requires reassurance around vehicle condition, legitimacy, service quality, deposits, insurance and local delivery. The first viewport offers premium styling but little evidence that the operator is trustworthy or operationally established.
issues.evidence: The objective scan reports trustSignalCount of 0. In the supplied screenshots there are no visible reviews, ratings, customer logos, operating-history statements, insurance/deposit guidance, delivery promise or verified local business signal.
issues.observed: The visitor is asked to submit dates and contact Mfinity without receiving enough proof to justify a high-value commitment.
issues.expected: Reference-quality execution would pair the luxury presentation with concise, credible operational proof and transparent rental expectations.
issues.location: Homepage hero and the immediately visible mobile content below the form.
issues.recommendation: Add a compact trust layer near the primary CTA: verified review rating, local operating statement, concierge response time, delivery coverage, maintenance standard and a concise deposit/insurance explanation. Use specific verifiable claims rather than generic adjectives.

issues.title: The desktop hero does not visibly sell the product
issues.detail: The first desktop viewport is dominated by near-black space, while the featured vehicle panel is small and visually secondary. A luxury rental site must make the cars themselves the strongest first-viewport signal.
issues.evidence: In the desktop screenshot, the main hero area behind “Luxury in every kilometer.” is effectively black and does not reveal a vehicle. The only recognizable vehicle reference is the small Ferrari 488 Spyder information panel on the right.
issues.observed: The user sees an abstract dark composition and pricing copy before seeing a compelling car image.
issues.expected: Reference-quality execution would show a sharp, high-impact vehicle image or clearly inspectable vehicle-led composition in the first viewport, while preserving the minimal luxury aesthetic.
issues.location: Desktop homepage hero, center and right side of the first viewport.
issues.recommendation: Use a high-resolution, clearly recognizable hero vehicle image as the primary visual anchor. Keep overlays restrained and ensure the featured model is visually connected to the image rather than represented mainly by a text panel.

issues.title: The mobile hero image is too blurred and poorly cropped
issues.detail: The mobile screenshot uses a heavily defocused background where the car is only partially visible at the bottom-right. This creates atmosphere but prevents the visitor from evaluating the actual rental product.
issues.evidence: The mobile hero background is visibly blurred across the full viewport, with the vehicle body cropped and obscured behind the form and dark overlay.
issues.observed: The image reads as generic motion or lifestyle texture rather than a premium car that a customer can desire and identify.
issues.expected: Reference-quality mobile imagery should preserve vehicle recognition, body shape, finish and model desirability even when cropped for a narrow viewport.
issues.location: Mobile homepage hero background.
issues.recommendation: Replace the atmospheric crop with a mobile-specific vehicle composition. Position the car prominently, reduce blur and use art direction that keeps the grille, silhouette or distinctive bodywork visible above or beside the form.

issues.title: Pricing transparency is incomplete and inconsistently contextualized
issues.detail: The Ferrari panel shows “From €1,400 / day,” but the form does not provide any pricing expectation and the supporting text qualifies deposits and longer rentals only in small copy. This can create uncertainty at the point of enquiry.
issues.evidence: The desktop featured panel contains “From €1,400 / day,” “Deposit €7,000” and “longer rentals on request.” The form itself provides no pricing cue, and no equivalent pricing information is visible in the mobile first viewport.
issues.observed: A customer can discover a headline daily rate but not understand what determines the final cost, whether rates vary by season or duration, or what is included.
issues.expected: Reference-quality rental presentation would make starting rates, deposit expectations, inclusions and quote variability easy to compare without forcing the visitor to infer the commercial model.
issues.location: Desktop featured vehicle panel; mobile hero form and supporting copy.
issues.recommendation: Standardize pricing presentation across vehicle cards and detail pages. Add “from” context, rental duration assumptions, deposit, insurance and delivery inclusions near the price, with a concise link to full rental terms.

issues.title: Vehicle discovery is visually underpowered in the first viewport
issues.detail: The site has many vehicle routes, but the supplied hero view gives the visitor only one small featured vehicle panel and no strong visual inventory cue. The secondary goal of vehicle discovery is therefore subordinate to the brand statement.
issues.evidence: The desktop screenshot shows a single text-led Ferrari panel occupying a narrow right column. The mobile screenshot does not show the featured vehicle panel in the first viewport, and the visible background vehicle is not inspectable.
issues.observed: Visitors who arrive wanting to browse cars must rely on the navigation or scroll beyond the hero, with limited immediate understanding of fleet breadth or categories.
issues.expected: Reference-quality execution would expose a concise but compelling fleet preview: recognizable vehicle imagery, model, category and starting rate, with an obvious path to compare or browse all cars.
issues.location: Homepage hero and first collection transition.
issues.recommendation: Increase the visual weight of the featured vehicle or introduce a compact first-viewport fleet rail with model, category, price-from and availability action. Preserve the editorial layout but make discovery possible without depending on navigation alone.

issues.title: Luxury positioning is stronger than the operational value proposition
issues.detail: The copy communicates mood and location well, but does not sufficiently answer why a customer should choose Mfinity over another Marbella rental provider.
issues.evidence: The primary copy is “Luxury in every kilometer.” and “Supercars, performance cars and premium mobility for Marbella and the Costa del Sol.” The visible supporting proof is limited to “Nueva Andalucía base,” “regular inspections & maintenance” and “direct local contact.”
issues.observed: The language is polished but generic. It does not clearly communicate delivery, concierge service, booking speed, airport or hotel handoff, fleet condition, flexibility or customer support standards.
issues.expected: Reference-quality content would retain the cinematic tone while adding specific, decision-useful differentiators tied to the Marbella rental context.
issues.location: Hero supporting copy and the visible mobile trust/value text below the form.
issues.recommendation: Add concrete service claims that can be substantiated, such as hotel/villa delivery areas, airport collection, concierge availability, response time, minimum rental terms and maintenance standards. Keep them short and operational rather than adding more brand language.

issues.title: The interface has some default control and template signals beneath the premium art direction
issues.detail: The surrounding composition is bespoke, but the availability form uses familiar standard input styling and the mobile CTA stack feels like a generic two-button block. This creates a gap between the editorial hero and the interaction layer.
issues.evidence: The mobile form is a rectangular black bordered panel with standard date fields, a select row and a large white button. The lower “WHATSAPP” and “RENT A CAR” controls are equal-weight rectangular blocks with limited differentiation in the screenshot. The objective scan reports an inconsistentButtonRatio of 0.3673.
issues.observed: The form is functional and legible, but not fully integrated into the luxury rental experience. The competing actions do not establish a clear primary versus secondary path.
issues.expected: Reference-quality execution would retain the strong contrast but use a more intentional control hierarchy, tighter component consistency and action labels aligned to the actual booking process.
issues.location: Mobile hero form and CTA block immediately below it; global button system.
issues.recommendation: Define one dominant reservation action, make WhatsApp a clearly secondary concierge option, and harmonize border, typography, spacing and hover/active treatment across all CTAs. Ensure the form feels like part of the same designed system as the hero.

issues.title: The mobile first screen is vertically overloaded before vehicle content begins
issues.detail: The mobile hero combines large headline typography, supporting copy, a three-part availability form, explanatory paragraphs, operational claims and another CTA block. This delays the fleet and reduces scan efficiency on the device most likely to be used while traveling.
issues.evidence: The supplied 390px-wide screenshot extends through the availability form, explanatory text, service claims and the beginning of “VEHICLE CARE” and “FLEET STANDARD” before the vehicle collection is visible.
issues.observed: The user must move through a long text-and-form sequence before reaching the actual cars, while the hero image itself is not usable for discovery.
issues.expected: Reference-quality mobile UX would preserve the booking CTA early but compress supporting content and reveal the first vehicle or fleet entry sooner.
issues.location: Mobile homepage from hero headline through the beginning of the next section.
issues.recommendation: Keep the form prominent, but reduce repeated explanatory copy, move secondary proof into compact rows or an accordion, and bring a recognizable vehicle card or collection preview into the next visible section.

issues.title: The brand identity is not consistently resolved across desktop and mobile
issues.detail: The desktop screenshot presents “MFINITY · MARBELLA” as a text lockup, while mobile shows a separate ornate Mfinity emblem. The two treatments do not immediately read as one tightly controlled luxury brand system.
issues.evidence: Desktop uses a minimalist text-based label in the hero and no obvious logo in the visible left navigation area. Mobile uses a white crest-like logo at top-left.

issues.expected: Reference-quality branding would use a consistent logo system with intentional desktop and mobile variants, shared proportions and a clear relationship to the wordmark.
issues.location: Desktop top navigation/hero label and mobile top navigation.
issues.recommendation: Establish a unified wordmark and emblem usage rule. Ensure the desktop and mobile headers share the same brand recognition, even if the compact mobile mark is retained.

aiReview.summary: Mfinity presents a polished dark luxury direction with strong typography, restrained navigation and a clear availability enquiry module. However, the execution currently feels closer to a premium automotive concept site than a high-converting Marbella rental operation. The most important weaknesses are the lack of a visible vehicle on desktop, an overly blurred and poorly inspectable hero image on mobile, limited trust proof, and a booking path that remains an enquiry rather than a sufficiently explicit reservation journey.
strengths: The visual language is disciplined and broadly appropriate for luxury car rental: black-and-white palette, generous spacing, uppercase microcopy and large editorial typography communicate confidence and premium positioning.
The desktop hero establishes the market clearly with “MFINITY · MARBELLA” and “Supercars, performance cars and premium mobility for Marbella and the Costa del Sol.”
The availability module is placed in the first viewport and includes useful initial inputs for dates and vehicle selection.
The desktop composition has a strong left-to-right hierarchy: brand positioning, primary headline, supporting copy, availability form and featured vehicle panel.
The mobile layout is responsive and avoids horizontal overflow, with large tap-friendly form controls and a prominent enquiry action.
The site has a broad vehicle inventory with dedicated detail routes, supporting vehicle discovery beyond the homepage.

The automated evidence indicates strong baseline implementation quality: fast loading, no failed requests, no console errors, valid heading structure, accessible form labeling and no broken internal links.

issues.title: The visit action is weaker than the menu action
issues.detail: The business primary goal is to drive visits or contact, but the most visually dominant CTA is “Descubrir la carta.” “Visítanos hoy” is rendered as a smaller text link with a thin underline, while “Contacto” is visually secondary in the header.
issues.evidence: In the desktop screenshot, the filled CTA is the largest action in the hero; “VISÍTANOS HOY” is a low-emphasis text link. The objective scan reports 3 primary CTAs but 0 booking signals and only contact signals, with no stronger visit or reservation mechanism identified.
issues.observed: The page prioritizes menu discovery over the immediate action most valuable to the business. A visitor who already wants to come needs to infer where to find practical details.
issues.expected: A premium café homepage should make the visit path equally prominent, with a direct location/hours CTA and, where relevant, clear contact, directions, reservation or WhatsApp behavior.
issues.location: Hero CTA group and top-right header navigation.
issues.recommendation: Promote “Visítanos” to a filled or equally weighted CTA and link directly to a visit section containing address, map directions, opening hours and contact options. Preserve the menu CTA as the parallel discovery action.

issues.title: Location clarity is too low for a destination café
issues.detail: “Puerto Banús” and “Marbella · Spain” establish the region, but the first viewport does not give the practical location information needed to decide to visit. There is no visible street address, landmark, map cue or directions affordance in the hero.
issues.evidence: The screenshots show only the geographic labels “PUERTO BANÚS · PÂTISSERIE & CAFÉ” and “MARBELLA · SPAIN.” The objective scan identifies a separate `visita.html` page but does not identify a prominent address or map signal in the critical homepage journey.
issues.observed: The brand communicates where it is broadly, but not where it is operationally. This is especially limiting for tourists and visitors navigating Puerto Banús, where proximity and exact location materially affect conversion.
issues.expected: The first screen or the immediate next section should expose the exact address, a recognizable local anchor and a one-tap directions action.
issues.location: Hero eyebrow, bottom-left location label and visit journey.
issues.recommendation: Add a compact location strip immediately below the hero or within the hero footer: exact address, Puerto Banús landmark/context, opening hours and “Cómo llegar” / map action.

issues.title: The product proposition is asserted more than demonstrated
issues.detail: The phrase “No sugar. Same taste.” is memorable, but the hero image is primarily an interior photograph. The actual pâtisserie selection is visible only indirectly through a distant display case and a cropped table setting.
issues.evidence: The desktop screenshot is dominated by the café interior; pastries appear small in the display case and partially cropped in the foreground. The scan reports 8 images overall, but the homepage evidence does not show a clear product-led selection module or individual product discovery in the first viewport.
issues.observed: The site sells premium sugar-free pâtisserie, yet the strongest visual proof is the venue rather than the products, textures and signature items that create appetite and perceived value.
issues.expected: A premium pâtisserie should show close, well-lit product photography with enough detail to understand the assortment, craftsmanship and reasons to visit.
issues.location: Homepage hero and initial visual narrative.
issues.recommendation: Follow the hero with a product-led section featuring 3 to 6 signature items, close crops, names, concise descriptions and a clear route to the full menu. Ensure the photography shows texture and finish rather than relying on the distant display case.

issues.title: The mobile hero gives too much vertical space to the image before practical content
issues.detail: The mobile composition is visually impressive but requires substantial scrolling before the visitor reaches anything beyond the hero. The header, language switcher, contact control, headline, body copy, two CTAs and location label occupy almost the entire first screen.
issues.evidence: The mobile screenshot shows a very tall hero with the practical footer label only near the bottom. The scan reports strong mobile technical metrics and no overflow, but those measurements do not address information prioritization or scroll efficiency.
issues.observed: The primary visit information is not available at the point of decision. The visual design is adapted to mobile dimensions, but the business journey is not equally optimized for mobile intent.
issues.expected: Mobile users should see a clear route to menu and visit details quickly, with the next useful content hinted or exposed without requiring a full-screen editorial sequence.
issues.location: Mobile homepage hero and header.
issues.recommendation: Reduce the mobile hero height or add a compact practical information band immediately after the primary actions with address, hours and directions. Keep the atmospheric image while shortening the distance to task completion.

issues.title: The messaging is elegant but not sufficiently specific about the offer
issues.detail: The copy frames sugar-free pâtisserie as a philosophy, but gives limited concrete information about what visitors can buy and why the experience is different beyond the absence of sugar.
issues.evidence: The visible copy includes “Pastelería artesanal, café y una forma más consciente...” and headings such as “Experiencia premium,” “Pastelería consciente” and “Innovación real.” These are broad positioning statements; the scan reports only 439 words and no trust signals.
issues.observed: The tone is premium, but several phrases could apply to many wellness or specialty café brands. The copy does not quickly answer which products are signature, whether the range is fully sugar-free, how taste is achieved, or what a first visit should include.
issues.expected: Content should pair the emotional brand line with concrete product and experience details that make the proposition credible and memorable.
issues.location: Hero supporting copy and concept/value-proposition sections.
issues.recommendation: Replace or supplement generic category language with specific proof points: signature pâtisserie, coffee and beverage offer, production approach, dietary scope, chef/founder expertise and what makes the Puerto Banús experience worth a visit.

issues.title: The hero image is atmospheric but visually busy behind the headline
issues.detail: The interior contains shelves, signage, counters, reflections, hanging lights and tableware. The dark overlay improves contrast, but the headline still competes with the display case and the large “NO SUGAR / SAME TASTE” wall text behind it.
issues.evidence: In the desktop screenshot, the wall lettering sits directly behind the left side of the hero and partially echoes the foreground headline. On mobile, the crop places the headline over the glass display case and food imagery, creating multiple competing text and visual layers.
issues.observed: The image feels authentic and premium, but the headline does not have a sufficiently controlled visual field. The repeated “NO SUGAR” message in the background reduces hierarchy rather than reinforcing it.
issues.expected: Hero photography should provide a deliberate area of calm for the brand message, with the product or venue remaining legible without competing typography in the source image.
issues.location: Hero background, especially left half of desktop and center-left mobile crop.
issues.recommendation: Use a crop with quieter background behind the copy, reposition the text into a calmer region, or select a hero image where the signage does not duplicate the headline. Keep the product and venue context visible elsewhere in the frame.

issues.title: There is no visible trust layer supporting the premium claim
issues.detail: The site communicates premium positioning and innovation but does not visibly reinforce it with customer proof, recognitions, press, partner credibility, dietary reassurance or other trust signals.
issues.evidence: The objective scan explicitly reports `trustSignalCount: 0`. The screenshots show no review count, awards, press mention, social proof, ingredient/dietary reassurance or clear evidence of customer adoption.
issues.observed: For a newer or differentiated sugar-free concept, the visitor is asked to accept “premium,” “artisanal” and “innovation real” primarily as brand language.
issues.expected: Reference-quality execution would provide concise, credible proof near the proposition or before the visit decision, without turning the page into a crowded testimonial template.
issues.location: Homepage content following the hero and concept messaging.
issues.recommendation: Add one restrained proof module: verified reviews, a credible founder/chef credential, press recognition, or a concise ingredient/production standard. Keep claims specific and evidence-based.

issues.title: The visual identity is distinctive, but some controls still read as generic web UI
issues.detail: The outlined pill-shaped “CONTACTO” control and understated navigation are serviceable, but they do not fully express the crafted editorial identity established by the logo and display typography.
issues.evidence: The desktop and mobile screenshots show a standard rounded outline contact button and small uppercase navigation. The objective scan also reports an inconsistent button ratio of 0.3077, indicating multiple interactive treatments across the site.
issues.observed: The brand system is strongest in the hero typography and photography; the utility controls feel more like a default luxury-template layer and create a slight mismatch in finish.
issues.expected: Navigation and CTAs should share a deliberate system of shape, spacing, weight and interaction states, with primary actions clearly differentiated from utility links.
issues.location: Header contact button, hero CTA group and site-wide link treatments.
issues.recommendation: Define a tighter action hierarchy: one primary visit/menu treatment, one secondary text-link treatment and one utility contact treatment. Align border radius, padding, type weight and arrow/icon behavior across pages.

issues.detail: The navigation uses very small, widely tracked uppercase labels, and the scan identifies three tiny interactive targets, including “CARTA,” “ERIC” and “LEGAL.” Their 44px height is technically usable, but the narrow widths and 12px text make them visually easy to miss.

issues.recommendation: Increase label size or weight modestly, expand horizontal hit areas, and provide a clear active state. Keep the editorial uppercase style only where it does not compromise discoverability.

aiReview.summary: Zùsto presents a polished, premium-looking first impression with strong venue photography, distinctive typography and a clear sugar-free positioning. However, the experience currently feels more like a brand statement than a high-performing café website: the product is not shown with enough appetite-led detail, the visit path is under-emphasized, and the mobile hero sacrifices practical navigation and content clarity for atmosphere. The automated scores are strong because the implementation is technically clean, but reference-quality execution for a premium pâtisserie would make the food, location, opening hours and next action substantially more immediate.
strengths: The hero immediately communicates the venue, the Puerto Banús context and the core proposition: “No sugar. Same taste.”
The interior image is relevant and authentic rather than generic stock photography, and it establishes a credible premium café environment.
Typography creates a distinctive editorial identity. The serif display treatment gives the brand more character than a default café template.
The primary menu CTA is visible above the fold and the secondary “Visítanos hoy” path supports the stated visit goal.
The site has a coherent navigation model covering concept, menu, founder, visit and contact pages.
The visual system is restrained and premium without relying on excessive gradients, decorative blobs or generic card layouts.
Objective evidence supports strong technical delivery: fast load times, no layout shift, no failed requests, no overflow, valid heading structure and complete image alt coverage.

There are no visible client names, fleet/capacity facts, operating experience, testimonials, safety or compliance indicators, response expectations, or case-study outcomes in the supplied first-view evidence.
issues.evidence: The scan finds only one trust signal across the page. The 527-word page has a strong proposition but no measured evidence of an operating record in the provided screenshots.

issues.expected: Reference-quality professional-services pages give decision-makers concise, specific validation near the first CTA and route them to credible evidence.

issues.title: The hero image is too dark to function as persuasive product evidence
issues.detail: The image establishes mood, but the vehicle is materially obscured by the black overlay, particularly on mobile where only fragmented red bodywork and a wheel are visible behind large text and panels. For a specialist transport operator, prospective buyers need to inspect the vehicle quality, scale and deployment context immediately.
issues.evidence: Both screenshots show a dense black overlay across the hero. The mobile crop makes the train difficult to read as a complete, premium vehicle; the red body is partially visible but key detail is lost.
issues.observed: The hero reads first as a dark luxury/editorial composition and only second as a transport-services offer.
issues.expected: Reference-quality execution would retain legible vehicle form, finish and context while using a controlled overlay only behind text. It would make the operational product visibly desirable and credible.
issues.location: Homepage hero, especially the mobile hero background.
issues.recommendation: Use a brighter, cleaner image treatment or position the text over a localized dark gradient. Choose a crop showing the full vehicle and passengers, destination, guide or municipal/event setting so the visual proves both the product and its use case.

issues.title: Mobile hero spends too much first-journey space on decorative project metadata
issues.detail: After two large CTAs, the mobile screenshot dedicates a substantial vertical block to “Project Brief / 01” and four metadata rows. This pushes discovery of services and portfolio content far below the fold, even though portfolio discovery is a stated secondary goal.
issues.evidence: The mobile hero occupies roughly two full viewport heights before the next section. The metadata block is visually as substantial as the actual CTA area.
issues.observed: A mobile visitor must scroll through internal-looking presentation material before reaching meaningful supporting content.
issues.expected: Reference-quality mobile design would keep the first screen focused on proposition, proof and one primary action, then expose the next substantive section promptly.
issues.location: Mobile homepage hero, below “Ver vehículos”.
issues.recommendation: Remove the project-brief treatment from the homepage hero or reduce it to one concise proof line. Bring the first service/portfolio section into view immediately after the CTA, and reserve project specifications for a case-study or vehicle page.

issues.title: Lead generation is routed through a generic budget CTA without visible qualification or reassurance
issues.detail: “Solicitar presupuesto” is clear, but it provides no indication of what the enquiry captures, how quickly the team responds, what information is needed, or whether the offer applies to rental, sale, municipal projects and events. No form is present on the homepage.
issues.evidence: The scan reports two primary CTAs, zero homepage forms, zero booking signals and six contact links. The critical journey works technically, but the visible entry point is a generic destination-page handoff.
issues.observed: The user can request a quote, but the CTA does little to reduce friction for distinct buyer types or clarify the next step.
issues.expected: Reference-quality lead capture would frame the next action around the buyer's goal, state a useful response expectation and provide a low-friction first step.
issues.location: Desktop navigation CTA and hero CTA; mobile hero CTA.
issues.recommendation: Use a context-rich CTA such as “Cuéntenos su proyecto” or “Solicite una propuesta para su municipio o evento,” with concise reassurance beneath it. Provide a short, clearly structured enquiry form or selector on the destination page for rental, purchase, event and municipal needs.

issues.title: Critical navigation and interface text are materially undersized
issues.detail: The design uses small uppercase display labels so aggressively that important navigation and action text becomes difficult to scan, especially in a professional-services context that may include public-sector decision-makers and mixed-age users.
issues.evidence: The scan identifies 96 tiny-text elements, representing 38% of visible elements. Desktop navigation is measured at 9.5px; several CTA and inline-link labels are 8.5-9px. It also flags 19 undersized tap targets out of 23 interactive targets.
issues.observed: The desktop navigation, kicker, inline links and CTA labels look refined at screenshot scale but sacrifice legibility and practical interaction comfort.
issues.expected: Reference-quality execution would preserve the editorial character while keeping essential interface text comfortably readable and interactive controls at accessible target dimensions.
issues.location: Desktop header, hero kicker/buttons, inline links and footer; associated mobile controls.
issues.recommendation: Set navigation and button labels to a substantially more readable minimum, use sentence case where appropriate, and increase the padding/height of navigation and text links. Retain small type only for genuinely secondary, nonessential metadata.

issues.title: The project-brief visual language feels imported from a presentation template rather than tied to buyer value
issues.detail: The vertical rule, “Project Brief / 01,” numbered slider line and metadata table create visual polish, but they do not explain a case, a route or a customer outcome. “Ámbito / Base / Modalidad / Enfoque” mostly restates broad company facts.
issues.evidence: The desktop hero includes a lower-right project-brief table and a bottom “01” carousel-style marker; the mobile version expands this into a dominant information block. The content does not identify an actual project or result.
issues.observed: Decorative interface conventions compete with the central service proposition while adding limited decision support.
issues.expected: Reference-quality design would use that visual weight for a real proof point, case-study result, fleet specification or service selector with a clear commercial purpose.
issues.location: Homepage hero, lower-right on desktop and below CTAs on mobile.
issues.recommendation: Replace the generic brief with a real featured case such as a named city/event, route length, passenger capacity and operational result, or remove it and use the space to expose the next content section.

issues.title: The positioning is broad but the first screen does not prioritize the buyer paths
issues.detail: The copy addresses cities, events, municipalities and venues in one sentence. These audiences have materially different needs, procurement cycles and proof requirements, yet the hero offers one generic quote path and a vehicle path.
issues.evidence: The heading samples identify four target contexts, while the visible hero presents a single generic statement and CTA pair. The hero labels also combine tourism, rental, sales and projects.
issues.observed: The offer reads as broad capability coverage rather than a deliberately organized specialist service.
issues.expected: Reference-quality service design would help each high-value audience recognize its path and relevant proof immediately.
issues.location: Homepage hero and primary navigation.
issues.recommendation: Introduce clearly labeled routes for municipal/tourism operations, event hire, fleet sales and bespoke projects below the proposition, each with an outcome-led one-line description and appropriate proof.

issues.title: Legal and privacy reassurance is absent from the scanned page
issues.detail: For a Spanish lead-generation business, especially one likely to deal with municipalities and corporate events, missing privacy and legal links weakens credibility at the point where buyers are asked to enquire.
issues.evidence: The objective scan reports no privacy link and no legal link. It also records a security/trust score of 75.4 despite successful HTTPS and no failed requests.
issues.observed: The site appears commercially active but omits expected footer-level trust and compliance destinations.
issues.expected: Reference-quality lead-generation execution would make privacy, legal notice and cookie information easy to locate, with contact ownership and company details presented clearly.
issues.location: Homepage footer and the quote/contact journey.
issues.recommendation: Add clearly visible footer links to Política de privacidad, Aviso legal and cookie information, plus verifiable company/contact details appropriate to the business.

issues.title: Some imagery lacks alternative text
issues.detail: The page relies on transport and destination imagery to communicate its offer, but not all images have alternative text. This loses useful context for assistive-technology users and makes the content less complete.
issues.evidence: Two of seven images are missing alt text (28.6%), including a YouTube thumbnail and an Écija image.
issues.observed: Relevant visual content has no programmatic explanation.
issues.expected: Reference-quality execution would give meaningful, concise alt text to informational images and mark purely decorative assets appropriately.
issues.location: Homepage image content, including the video thumbnail and Écija-related image.
issues.recommendation: Add descriptive Spanish alt text that identifies the vehicle, location or service context; use empty alt text only where an image is strictly decorative.

issues.title: Button treatments are not sufficiently systematized
issues.detail: The primary yellow CTA, outlined vehicle CTA and multiple small text-arrow links use differing proportions and label styles. Variation can support hierarchy, but here the measured inconsistency and very small labels make the action system feel less controlled than the art direction suggests.
issues.evidence: The scan measures an inconsistent button ratio of 0.39. Visible examples range from filled and outlined rectangular buttons to small uppercase text-arrow links.
issues.observed: The hierarchy is understandable, but action styling does not yet feel like a robust component system.
issues.expected: Reference-quality execution would use a limited, consistent action hierarchy with dependable label sizing, spacing and state behavior.
issues.location: Header, hero CTA group and section-level inline links.
issues.recommendation: Define primary, secondary and tertiary action patterns with consistent height, typography and arrow placement; reserve the filled yellow treatment for the single highest-priority action per context.

aiReview.summary: The homepage has a credible editorial direction and a strong subject-relevant hero image, but it currently prioritizes art direction over commercial clarity. It presents the service as an attractive concept rather than a proven specialist operation: the hero is too dark and sparse, type is frequently too small, the mobile first screen is excessively tall, and proof and lead-capture reassurance are largely absent. Performance and structural fundamentals are strong, but the visible experience falls below reference-quality professional-services execution.
strengths: The hero uses a real, relevant vehicle image rather than generic transport stock imagery, immediately anchoring the offer in the category.
The dark charcoal, white and warm yellow palette is coherent and gives the page a more considered identity than a default service-business template.
Desktop hero hierarchy is clear at a glance: service category, headline, supporting statement and budget CTA appear in a logical order.
The primary enquiry CTA is prominent and repeated in the main navigation and hero. On mobile it becomes a full-width, easily recognizable action.
The service framing addresses meaningful buyer contexts, including cities, events, town halls and venues, which supports the stated Spanish professional-services market.
The screenshots show orderly alignment, no evident overflow, and strong loading and layout-stability measurements.

issues.title: Trust is claimed but not demonstrated
issues.detail: The site references fifteen-plus years of local experience, real availability and qualified skippers, but there are no visible trust assets supporting those claims. In a high-value booking decision, especially for an unfamiliar operator, this materially lowers perceived credibility.
issues.evidence: The objective scan reports `trustSignalCount: 0`. issues.observed: Trust content is presented as unverified marketing copy rather than proof. The visitor has little reason to distinguish this operator from a lead-generation template or reseller.
issues.expected: Reference-quality charter sites make expertise and operational legitimacy easy to verify without forcing the visitor to search elsewhere.
issues.location: Homepage proof strip and broader conversion journey
issues.recommendation: Add specific evidence: verified review excerpts with source, captain or crew credentials, company history, insurance or safety standards where appropriate, marina or local operating details, and recognizable partner or accreditation marks if genuinely held.

issues.title: Pricing context is too narrow for a premium purchase decision
issues.detail: The homepage exposes one price reference for a Sunseeker 68, framed as “from €4,375 / 4h,” with low-season and VAT caveats. This is useful but insufficient for visitors comparing yacht types, dates and group sizes, and it risks creating uncertainty about the real booking range.
issues.evidence: Desktop proof strip shows only “Sunseeker 68 · from €4,375 / 4h” and “low season · 21% VAT excluded.” The scan identifies fleet links but no broader pricing context.
issues.observed: The visitor cannot quickly understand starting prices across the fleet, what is included, how seasonality affects pricing, or whether skipper, fuel, catering and VAT are included in the displayed figure.
issues.expected: Reference-quality execution gives enough pricing context to qualify enquiries while preserving the bespoke nature of the service.
issues.location: Homepage proof strip, fleet discovery and charter enquiry flow
issues.recommendation: Show indicative starting ranges or clear “from” pricing for each major yacht category, define inclusions and exclusions near the price, and explain that final pricing depends on date, duration, yacht and extras. Keep a direct enquiry CTA alongside the context.

issues.title: The copy is evocative but underdeveloped for fleet and experience discovery
issues.detail: The editorial headline and supporting paragraph establish mood, but the homepage copy does not quickly explain the practical differences between yacht types, experiences, destinations, inclusions or ideal use cases. The result is attractive but not especially informative for a considered purchase.
issues.evidence: The scan reports 678 words and a content score of 91.67, while the visible hero copy is primarily atmospheric. The available H2s, including “The yacht sets the scene. The day is what stays with you.” and “Three reference points.”, remain highly conceptual.
issues.observed: Visitors must navigate deeper into the site to answer basic qualification questions that could be addressed earlier: who each yacht suits, what can be done, how long trips run and what makes the operator different.
issues.expected: Luxury copy can remain concise and poetic while still providing concrete decision support for fleet, destinations, group size, occasion and charter format.
issues.location: Homepage hero and introductory sections
issues.recommendation: Add concise, scannable qualification copy around the fleet and experiences: capacity, best-for use case, typical duration, departure area, experience type and key inclusions. Retain the editorial voice as the framing layer rather than the only layer of information.

issues.title: Mobile hero loses the premium cinematic treatment
issues.detail: The mobile crop is substantially weaker than the desktop composition. The background becomes a flat blue-grey field, the logo and phone sit over a visually busy gradient-like image, and the large headline dominates without a corresponding sense of place.
issues.evidence: Mobile screenshot shows a pale blue-grey hero with limited image definition, while the desktop screenshot has a controlled black composition. The same brand experience therefore has noticeably different visual quality by viewport.
issues.observed: Mobile feels like a fallback crop rather than a deliberate art-directed composition. The hero image does not appear to be helping the user understand the product.
issues.expected: The mobile crop should retain a strong focal subject, clear depth and a deliberate relationship between image, headline and charter form.
issues.location: Homepage hero on mobile
issues.recommendation: Create a dedicated mobile image crop or responsive art direction that keeps the yacht and horizon legible. Rebalance the overlay and text placement so the background supports the headline instead of becoming an indistinct wash.

issues.title: The main CTA language is slightly indirect for the critical journey
issues.detail: “Find my charter” is elegant but less explicit than the action required from a visitor seeking a high-value booking. The site appears to collect an enquiry rather than provide instant inventory, so the CTA should set an accurate expectation.
issues.evidence: The hero CTA is “FIND MY CHARTER,” while the business primary goal is a charter enquiry or booking. The scan confirms one form and strong booking/contact signals but does not indicate live booking inventory.
issues.observed: The CTA makes the user infer whether they are checking availability, requesting a quote or starting a conversation.
issues.expected: Reference-quality conversion copy removes ambiguity at the decision point and communicates the next step in concrete terms.
issues.location: Hero form CTA and repeated booking CTAs
issues.recommendation: Test “Check availability,” “Request a charter quote” or “Plan your charter,” depending on the actual workflow. Add a short expectation-setting line near the CTA, such as response timing or what information the team will return.

issues.title: The hero selector presents as a booking form without enough immediate flexibility
issues.detail: The selector contains Guests, Date, Duration, Departure and The Day, but the visible defaults are highly specific: two guests, half day, Puerto Banus and “Private yacht day.” The form does not visibly communicate whether fields are editable menus, whether other departures are available, or which experiences can be selected.
issues.evidence: Desktop screenshot shows fixed-looking values in five adjacent fields; mobile shows the same values in a large 2-column grid. Only the date field visibly exposes an input affordance.
issues.observed: The interface may be functional, but visually it behaves more like a prefilled design component than a transparent availability or enquiry tool. Visitors may not understand the available option space before clicking the CTA.
issues.expected: A high-converting charter selector should make the interaction model and choice range obvious while keeping the first step lightweight.
issues.location: Homepage hero charter selector
issues.recommendation: Use clear select/date/input affordances and concise helper states, provide meaningful option labels, and make the CTA reflect the result, such as “Check availability” or “Request options,” when the form does not return live inventory.

issues.title: The interface has a recognizable premium template feel
issues.detail: The centered serif hero, uppercase eyebrow, thin rules, editorial section titles and segmented booking bar are coherent, but the composition is familiar enough to feel system-generated rather than unmistakably owned by a specific Marbella operator.
issues.evidence: Desktop screenshot relies on a standard luxury-editorial pattern: dark hero, centered oversized serif headline, uppercase tracking, white pill CTA, horizontal field strip and proof row. The objective scan also detects 38 colors, three font families and a 22.7% inconsistent-button ratio, suggesting some system variation underneath the polished surface.
issues.observed: The brand tone is credible but not yet distinctive. There is limited visible local character, yacht-specific art direction or signature interaction that would make the operator memorable.
issues.expected: Reference-quality work should retain restraint while introducing a few ownable details tied to Marbella, Puerto Banus, the fleet or the company’s service model.
issues.location: Homepage visual system, especially hero, CTA styling and proof strip
issues.recommendation: Strengthen proprietary art direction through distinctive photography, a more specific visual motif drawn from the marina or coastline, and tighter normalization of button treatments, type roles and spacing across pages.

issues.title: The mobile sticky action bar risks covering the experience content
issues.detail: The bottom-fixed “Plan a charter” and “WhatsApp” controls are useful conversion aids, but in the supplied mobile screenshot they occupy a substantial portion of the lower viewport and sit over the page flow. This can reduce visible content and create a persistent visual obstruction.
issues.evidence: Mobile screenshot shows a fixed-looking two-button bar across the bottom, while the page underneath continues into the proof content. The bar is large relative to the 780px-tall viewport.

issues.expected: Sticky conversion controls should remain accessible while preserving content visibility and clear primary/secondary hierarchy.
issues.location: Mobile bottom action bar
issues.recommendation: Reserve bottom safe-area space in the document, reduce the bar footprint where possible, make “Plan a charter” clearly primary, and consider collapsing or hiding the secondary WhatsApp action after the user reaches the enquiry form.

issues.detail: The scan identifies ten tiny text elements, including 11.5px phone/footer text and 10.4px section labels. While the objective accessibility checks pass, this is still visually weak for a luxury service where contact and legal clarity should feel deliberate and effortless.

aiReview.summary: A polished, restrained luxury direction with strong typography, clear navigation and a credible enquiry-oriented structure. However, the experience currently reads more like a high-end editorial template than a fully convincing luxury charter business: the yacht itself is absent from the first viewport, trust is asserted rather than evidenced, pricing context is thin, and the mobile hero loses much of the intended cinematic quality. The site is structurally strong, but not yet reference-quality for a premium charter operator.
strengths: Strong typographic contrast between the serif display headline and restrained sans-serif interface text.
Clear primary path through the hero charter selector, navigation, phone contact and repeated “Plan a charter” actions.
The positioning is immediately understandable: Marbella, Puerto Banus and Costa del Sol are prominent in the hero.
The visual system is disciplined and premium in tone, with controlled spacing, thin dividers and a restrained black, white and warm-neutral palette.
The mobile layout is intentionally adapted rather than simply compressed: the navigation collapses, the charter fields become a grid, and the sticky bottom actions support enquiry conversion.

The objective scan confirms solid structural fundamentals: one H1, valid internal links, no horizontal overflow, no console or network errors, accessible form controls and strong mobile technical results.

aiReview.summary: Marbella For Sale presents a polished, editorial luxury aesthetic with strong performance and technical foundations. The hero image, restrained palette and spacious composition communicate premium positioning effectively. However, the first viewport behaves more like a brand film cover than a property-discovery experience: the route to listings is visually secondary, the mobile navigation is overly compressed, and the imagery is too dark and heavily cropped to support confident property evaluation. The overall execution is strong, but it is not yet reference-quality for a premium real estate platform whose primary goal is enquiry.
strengths: The hero immediately signals Marbella and premium residential property through a large, high-quality villa image rather than generic marketing graphics.
The editorial visual direction is coherent: restrained typography, generous negative space, dark photographic treatment and minimal controls create a credible luxury tone.
The brand is highly visible in the first viewport on both desktop and mobile, with clear location and category recognition.
The page has a well-structured content outline, one H1, descriptive property headings, complete image alt coverage and no detected broken links or console errors.
Performance is excellent in the supplied measurements, with 596 ms desktop LCP, 356 ms mobile LCP and zero layout shift.
The site includes multiple enquiry routes such as 'Speak to an advisor', 'Private search' and 'Begin a private search', which aligns with a high-touch brokerage model.

issues.recommendation: Reduce the consent UI to a compact bottom banner on desktop and a restrained bottom sheet on mobile. Preserve clear accept, reject/manage and policy actions, but prevent it from covering the H1 or hero CTA. Recheck the first viewport with the banner open at both breakpoints.

aiReview.summary: La Bocana presents a polished premium waterfront mood with strong typography, restrained color, clear reservation access and excellent technical execution. The main weakness is not the visual system itself, but the experience around it: the cookie panel dominates the first viewport, the mobile hero is poorly protected from obstruction, and the site communicates atmosphere more strongly than concrete restaurant value, trust, menu detail and location confidence. It feels close to premium reference quality, but not yet fully editorial or conversion-optimized for a high-consideration Puerto Banus dining decision.
